common_name: Wild Swan Windflower (Long-Blooming Blue-Backed White Anemone)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike most Japanese anemones, Wild Swan blooms almost continuously from late spring through fall rather than only in late summer.

directions: This Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit selection carries large single white flowers whose petals are washed with slate-blue on the reverse, giving each bloom a striking two-toned effect that twists visibly in the wind. Unlike the aggressively spreading Anemone x hybrida cultivars, Wild Swan forms a well-behaved, non-invasive clump and rewards deadheading with repeat flushes of bloom from late spring right through the first hard frost. Site it in a spot with reliably moist soil, since it is less drought-tolerant than the fall-only Japanese anemones and will sulk if allowed to dry out during summer heat. Established clumps can be divided in spring every few years to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.

common_name: Königin Charlotte Japanese Anemone (Queen Charlotte Fall Anemone)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this 1898 German introduction is among the oldest and most reliably vigorous of the Japanese anemone cultivars.

directions: Introduced in 1898 and still widely grown, Königin Charlotte bears large, semi-double, clear silvery-pink flowers 3-4 inches across with a prominent boss of golden stamens, carried on strong branching stems above dark green, coarsely divided foliage from late summer into fall. It has held a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for its reliability and garden performance, tolerating both heavier clay soils and light shade better than many newer hybrids. Like other Japanese anemone cultivars it spreads steadily by shallow rhizomes to form an expanding colony over time, so give it room or plan to divide and share excess growth every few years. Leave the seed heads standing through winter for texture and wildlife interest before cutting back in early spring.

common_name: September Sprite Anemone (Dwarf Compact Fall-Blooming Windflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; its compact habit suits front-of-border spots and containers where taller Japanese anemones would overwhelm the space.

directions: A dwarf sport discovered on the older cultivar 'Praecox', September Sprite tops out at little more than knee height, far shorter than the typical 3-4 foot Japanese anemone, while still producing the same deep rose-pink, single to semi-double flowers with golden centers from late summer into fall. Its compact, well-branched habit makes it far less prone to flopping than taller cultivars and useful for the front of a shaded border or in large containers. It spreads more slowly and modestly by rhizomes than full-sized Japanese anemone selections, making it a better choice for smaller gardens where an aggressive spreader would be unwelcome. Cut stems back after frost and mulch new plantings their first winter to help clumps establish.

common_name: Blue Shades Grecian Windflower (Mixed Blue-Violet Anemone Blanda)

planting.note: Plant tubers in fall, after soaking briefly to rehydrate, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Blue Shades is a mixed strain spanning pale sky-blue to deep violet-blue, closer to the wild species than the named single-color selections.

directions: Soak the knobby tubers briefly in lukewarm water before planting, then set them 2 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Blue Shades produces daisy-like flowers spanning the natural range of the species from soft sky-blue through deeper violet-blue, giving plantings more color variation than the uniform named cultivars like 'White Splendour' or 'Radar'. It flowers in early to mid spring, closing at night and in cloudy weather, and gradually naturalizes by tuberous rhizomes into an expanding carpet before going dormant in early summer. It combines especially well with yellow daffodils and other early bulbs, where the blue tones read as a cool complement. Once established it needs essentially no maintenance and resents being disturbed, so choose a permanent planting site.

common_name: Mona Lisa Anemone (Large Single-Flowered Poppy Anemone Strain)

planting.note: Soak corms briefly before planting 2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; in mild-winter zones 7-10 plant in fall for winter-to-spring bloom, and in colder zones start corms in late winter for spring or summer bloom.

directions: Developed as a commercial cut-flower strain, Mona Lisa produces extra-large single blooms 3-4 inches across on notably long, sturdy stems, sold as separate colors of red, blue, purple, pink, and white rather than the mixed-color runs typical of older strains like De Caen. Soak the small, irregular corms for a few hours before planting to speed rehydration, and set them 2 inches deep with the pointed growing point downward. Like other poppy anemones it performs best where winters are mild and springs are long and cool, going summer-dormant once heat arrives, so gardeners in colder regions should treat corms as a spring-planted annual for early summer bloom. Its long stems and clean color separation make it a favorite among cut-flower growers for bunching and mixed bouquets.
